newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China set to endorse Hong Kong's leader-elect.
newsitem.headline: China set to endorse Hong Kong's leader-elect.

text.p: Hong Kong's newly anointed leader-in-waiting, Tung Chee-hwa, was set on Thursday to receive endorsement of his landslide victory by China.
The 59-year-old shipping magnate proved the overwhelming choice of a Beijing-vetted committee on Wednesday as the man to lead the British colony upon its transition to Chinese rule next year.
Tung, whose father fled the Chinese communist revolution in 1949, will take over the helm when the colony reverts to China in 201 days' time at midnight on June 30.
Tung had little time to savour his victory over two rivals on Wednesday.
Within hours of his victory, he travelled to China to prepare for a Thursday meeting of the influential caucus responsible for the transition of Hong Kong.
China called a session of its Preparatory Committee, the 150-strong body of prominent Hong Kong and Chinese citizens established to manage the handover of Hong Kong.

Foreign Minister Qian Qichen will chair the meeting in the southern boomtown of Shenzhen which would endorse Tung's role on the behalf of the central government in Beijing, a committee spokesman said.

Security was tight ahead of the morning session, reporters in Shenzhen said. They expect to see no repeat of the skirmishing and scuffling in Hong Kong on Wednesday from protesters denouncing the selection process as unrepresentative.

During the afternoon, the committee will begin what promises to be its most controversial task -- setting the ground rules for a Provisional Legislature in Hong Kong to replace the existing elected chamber.
China, angered by the reforms spearheaded by British Governor Chris Patten, vowed to neutralise them by dissolving Hong Kong's legislature when it takes control.
Navigating this potential minefield could prove Tung's biggest immediate headache.
About half the existing chamber has applied to join the Provisional Legislature, along with a slew of politicians who failed to win election in the polls in 1995, the first under the Patten reforms.

But opposition in Hong Kong to the new chamber is stiff and many people are deeply concerned about the confusion that may arise if two rival legislatures jockey for power in the final six months of British rule.
Hong Kong's Democratic Party, which fared the strongest in last year's polls, adamantly opposes China's plans which it describes as rolling back democratic reforms.
Its leaders say they are preparing to mount a legal challenge against the chamber which they denounce as unconstitutional.
Britain and its allies overseas have denounced China's plans as unnecessary and likely to damage confidence in the sensitive time around the handover.
Tung, who as a member of Patten's inner cabinet at the time, was a member of the colonial administration responsible for the democratic reforms which so angered China.

The tycoon, who turned to Beijing for a bailout when his family fleet ran into difficulty a decade ago, has since distanced himself from the reforms and supported the need for a provisional legislature.
